edits.walkthrough_append: Worked check: place three services on the hierarchy — a top consulting firm can survive only in Mumbai or Bengaluru where its clients are (high-order, few locations); a diagnostic laboratory serves a district town (middle order); a hair salon needs one street of customers (low order, everywhere). The pattern repeats worldwide: professional and business services concentrate, personal services diffuse. For the board examination, a question of the form 'distinguish personal, professional and business services' is answered with a definition line each, one example per class, and the threshold argument — the higher the order of the service, the larger the market it needs.

Worked check: name the work and the address together — genomics research in a Bengaluru laboratory, market-analytics teams crunching retail data in Gurugram, a think tank drafting climate policy in Delhi: each sells knowledge itself, not a service performed on a person or a thing. Their inputs are graduates and bandwidth; their products travel at the speed of a file. For the board examination, quaternary questions are answered with the definition, two sectors with examples (IT, R&D, consultancy, media), the contrast with tertiary — doing versus knowing — and the location logic of research parks and metro clustering.

Worked check: measure the divide three ways in one district — does the household have a connection (access)? does the member use it for banking and study or only entertainment (use)? does online presence convert into jobs and prices (benefit)? Each step re-sorts the same population. For the board examination, a digital-divide answer carries the definition, the three-layer divide with one Indian statistic-style illustration each — urban-rural connectivity, gender gaps in use, language content — and the closing feedback argument: development drives access, and access then drives development, so the gap compounds unless policy breaks it.

Worked check: sort one office tower floor by floor — ground-floor retail and banking counters (tertiary: routine service); middle floors of software engineers processing data (quaternary: knowledge work); the top floor where a board decides to close a plant on another continent (quinary: high-stakes decisions). The building is the sector ladder in concrete. For the board examination, the three-way distinction is answered with a definition each, one occupation per tier, and the closing argument that economies upgrade by internal differentiation — routine services everywhere, knowledge and decision work concentrated in the largest cities.

Worked check: convert physical distance into economic distance — a hill village thirty kilometres from the district town by a bad road takes three hours and a higher freight rate than a plain town ninety kilometres away on a highway; the nearer place is economically farther. That is what transport cost measures. For the board examination, a transport-and-development answer runs: definition and modes in a line each, the network idea of nodes and links, the worked example above, and the closing sentence that roads change prices, attendance and marriage markets — transport is development's first mover in remote regions.

Worked check: arbitrate one mode choice with the facts — moving 2,000 tonnes of coal a day over 500 kilometres: rail wins on cost per tonne-kilometre; delivering that coal the last ten kilometres to the plant: road wins on reach; building new rail through Himalayan terrain: construction and maintenance costs hand the argument to all-weather roads. For the board examination, land-transport questions are answered with the classification (national and state highways, district and village roads; gauge and route classes on rail), the density contrast between India's road-dominant freight and rail's bulk role, and the closing line that terrain, volume and jurisdiction decide the mode.

Worked check: price one tonne of steel two ways — a thousand kilometres by coastal shipping versus by rail-and-road: the sea leg costs a fraction and carries no rail congestion, but adds port handling and days of transit; for low-value bulk the sea wins, for urgent high-value cargo it does not. For the board examination, water-transport answers give the inland-ocean division, India's named national waterways and the twelve major ports with a west-east coast split, the merits (cheapest per tonne-kilometre, least fuel) against the limits (slow, channel-bound), and the closing line that ports and shipping lanes structure world trade.

Worked check: choose the mode for two cargoes — a transplant organ from Chennai to Delhi goes by air because minutes matter more than money; a consignment of marble slabs goes by rail because weight, not time, is the cost driver. Air transport's geography follows from that trade-off: hubs at metropolitan airports, thin routes dropped to regional carriers, freight reserved for the most time-sensitive goods. For the board examination, air-transport answers carry the advantages (speed, terrain-free routes, reach into landlocked and disaster-hit areas), the limitations (cost, energy, weather), and the mode-selection sentence closing with time-versus-cost-versus-nature-of-goods.

Worked check: take the Trans-Siberian as the case — Moscow to Vladivostok across eleven time zones, hauling timber, grain and minerals from the interior to the Pacific ports, and carrying settlers and manufactures back; the line built the towns along it, from Novosibirsk onward. Read its flows in two directions and the economic geography of the whole Siberian margin appears. For the board examination, trans-continental railway answers name one line in full (route, terminals, terrain crossed), the freight-and-settlement logic, and one parallel from the Trans-Canadian or Cape-to-Cairo plans, closing that such lines convert empty interiors into resource frontiers.

Worked check: read one highway against the terrain it crosses — the Trans-Canadian runs between two coasts but swings through the southern prairie corridor because permafrost and forest north of it would ruin the economics; the Pan-American Highway breaks at the Darien jungle, proof that even continental projects stop where swamp and politics agree to stop them. For the board examination, highway answers name two routes with terminals, give one engineering-or-political obstacle each, and close with the generalisation that routes thread the path of least resistance while linking the densest economic cores.

Worked check: solve one coverage problem three ways — laying cable to a thousand Himalayan villages costs more than launching capacity; mobile towers cannot hold line-of-sight across deep valleys; a satellite covers all of them at once, and proved it during the 2004 tsunami when terrestrial networks failed. For the board examination, satellite-communication answers give the working (uplink, transponder, downlink), the classes of orbit in a line, three advantages — terrain-independence, disaster resilience, wide-area broadcast — and the closing judgement that for vast, sparse or hazard-prone regions the satellite is not an alternative but the only viable option.

Worked check: follow one product's globalised journey — a phone designed in California, fabricated in Taiwan, assembled in Vietnam and sold in Europe: container shipping and air freight (transport) move it for pennies a unit; contracts, design files and payments travel by data networks (communication) in seconds. Neither half works without the other. For the board examination, a globalisation question is answered with the two-system metaphor — transport as circulation, communication as nervous signalling — one such product chain traced through its stages, and the closing line that distance has become cheap for goods and nearly free for information, which is what lets production scatter while control stays connected.

Worked check: compute and compare — Bihar with about 1,106 persons per square kilometre and Arunachal Pradesh with about 17 live under the same flag; divide population by area for each and the ratio is nearly sixty-five-fold. Then explain it with the three-layer argument: the plain's alluvial soil and perennial water support intensive agriculture; its riverine history built towns and roads; and Arunachal's forested hills support neither. For the board examination, density questions are answered with the formula, the 2011 national figure of 382, two contrasting states with computed values, and the closing sentence that density is the joint product of land's capacity and human effort upon it.

Worked check: explain one dense belt and one sparse zone by factor, not by adjective — the northern plains: fertile alluvium, assured water, temperate climate, and centuries of transport routes and irrigation investment; the Rajasthan desert: water scarcity capping every other advantage; the north-east: terrain and forest constraining both agriculture and access. For the board examination, a distribution-of-population answer earns marks in a fixed order: the physical factors with named examples, the socio-economic factors — irrigation, industry, urbanisation — each with one case, and the closing sentence that the pattern is nature's possibilities worked upon by human history and technology.

Worked check: read one phase arithmetically — between 1921 and 1951 growth accelerated as death rates began falling while birth rates stayed high; between 1951 and 1981 the same widening gap produced the fastest decadal growth (nearly 25 per cent); after 1991 growth eased below 22 per cent as fertility declined. For the board examination, growth-of-population questions ask for the phases with approximate rates and their causes — the 1921 year of the great demographic divide is the standard anchor — and answers earn the final mark by computing one decade's percentage from two census figures in the margin.

Worked check: place India's states on the transition map — Kerala and Tamil Nadu, with low birth and death rates, stand in the late third stage; Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, with higher birth rates, lag behind; the national aggregate is a middle transition. The variation itself is the lesson: the same country contains several demographic regimes. For the board examination, transition answers in the Indian context must go beyond the generic model: state the phases, place two named states at different stages with their vital rates, and close that transition here has been policy-shaped — literacy, health services, family planning — not automatic.

Worked check: read one pyramid's three tiers — a broad 0-14 base (about a third of India) means heavy child dependency and rising school demand; a 15-59 middle band above 60 per cent is the working-age window; a narrow 60-plus top signals that ageing pressures are still a generation away nationally, though already real in Kerala. For the board examination, age-structure answers are answered from the given diagram, never from memory alone: identify the shape, compute the dependency ratio from the tiers, and end by naming the dividend — and the schooling and jobs it presupposes — because the blueprint argument carries the marks.

Worked check: compute one gap correctly — the national literacy rate of 74.04 per cent in 2011 conceals a male-female gap of about 16 percentage points; subtract the two rates, state the gap, then explain it: daughters' schooling trades against household work and early marriage, especially in the plain states, while Kerala's near-universal female literacy shows the ceiling. For the board examination, literacy questions expect the definition (seven-plus, reads and writes with understanding), the national and gender figures, the regional extremes — Kerala at the top, and the states at the bottom named — and the link from female literacy to fertility and child health that closes the argument.

Worked check: apply the census tests and read the number — a settlement is urban if a municipality governs it, or it crosses 5,000 people, 400 persons per square kilometre, and three-quarters of male workers in non-farm work. On those tests only about 31 per cent of Indians were urban in 2011, against Goa's 62 per cent and Himachal's 10 per cent. For the board examination, rural-urban composition answers state the criteria, give the national and one state figure, and explain the trend: migration and natural growth feed towns, with the closing line that India urbanises slowly because agriculture still holds its workforce.

Worked check: classify and explain one stream — a Uttar Pradesh farm hand moving to a Surat textile mill crosses state lines for work: rural-to-urban, interstate, employment-driven; the 2011 census counted about 456 crore lifetime migrants, with marriage as the largest female reason and work the largest male reason. For the board examination, migration answers define migration, run the four-way classification (place, distance, time, reason), give one worked stream with its causes — push of stagnant fields, pull of urban wages — and close with the consequences: remittances home, slums at destination, and remittance states grown dependent on them.

Worked check: read the policy as a checklist against a state — where child marriage persists, schooling incentives attack the cause; where immunisation lags, the midwife's outreach matters more than the slogan; where son preference distorts, the ban on sex-selection tests plus girls' education schemes act together. The National Population Policy's direction — services before targets — is exactly what this state-wise reading shows. For the board examination, NPP-2000 answers list the objective with its 2010 date and the socio-demographic goals in three lines, then evaluate with one state example, closing that population policy works only against local barriers, not national averages.

Worked check: classify two settlements from site alone — a hamlet strung along a desert oasis lives by its spring and stays small and compact; a riverside town spreads in streets along the levee and grows into trade. Form follows the resource, function follows the wider economy. For the board examination, a settlement-types answer runs: definition, the rural-urban division with the census criteria in one line each, and two named examples where terrain or water plainly dictated the form — the examiner is reading whether you can move from definition to site logic without drifting into generalities.

Worked check: test a fast-growing census town against the four criteria — population 9,000 (crosses 5,000); density 500 per square kilometre (crosses 400); three-quarters of male workers in trade and transport (crosses the 75 per cent non-farm bar); governed still by a panchayat — it is a census town, urban by function but rural by administration, and the census counts it urban anyway. For the board examination, definition-of-urban questions are answered by listing the statutory and census routes separately, running the given case through the three demographic-functional tests, and closing that the definition exists precisely so that planning and comparison stand on one measurable line.

Worked check: compute the shift and its meaning — with 31.2 per cent urban in 2011 against about 11 per cent in 1901, India's urban share has nearly tripled in 110 years, yet remains far below the world average; the absolute numbers, though, put India among the largest urban populations on earth. For the board examination, urbanisation answers give the definition (share of urban population rising, not just numbers), the drivers — migration, natural growth, and reclassification of new census towns — the national figures with two states contrasted, and the closing structural point: urbanisation tracks the workforce's shift out of agriculture, so slow urbanisation is agriculture's shadow.
